8.2.4 Heat-Recovery Combined-Cycle Combustion Turbine
The heat-recovery combined-cycle combustion turbine combines a conventional steam turbine with one or more simple cycle combustion turbines. A large portion of the thermal energy contained in the combustion turbine exhaust gases is recovered to supply a portion or all of the heat required to produce steam for the steam-turbine portion of the unit. In its usual form, the two types of turbines employed in a combined-cycle unit drive separate electric generators.
The principal point of superiority of the combined-cycle unit over the simple-cycle unit is the higher thermal efficiency of the combined-cycle unit. Higher efficiency results in lower production costs for electric energy, lower consumption of irreplaceable fuels, and less pollution.
The increased efficiency of the combined-cycle plant is not obtained without sacrifices. When compared with the simple-cycle combustion turbine, the combined-cycle unit: (1) costs more per kilowatt of capacity, (2) requires a longer lead time for construction, (3) requires longer to go from a cold start to full-load, (4) requires condenser cooling water and boiler feed water for the steam unit, and (5) is more complex (which results in higher maintenance costs and lower reliability).
8.2.5 Coal-Fired Steam Peaking and Intermediate Load Plant
Coal-fired steam units with ratings near 300 megawatts which are specifically designed for fast start-up and load-following service have heat rates and thermal efficiencies approximating those of the new generation of combined cycle combustion turbine units. They can be shut down in about 2 minutes but require a minimum of 1 hour from light-off to full-load after an overnight shut-down. Older units are maintained at operating temperature or hotbank (to reduce maintenance costs) during overnight shutdowns. The new generation of load-following steam plants which are not maintained at hotbank on overnight shutdown maintain the condenser vacuum to exclude oxygen from the system.
